crashes.note: the term is quoted in the modern literature; ancient passage not identified

factions.name: russata
factions.source: Tertullian De spect. 9; Pliny NH 7.186 (a supporter of the Reds on a charioteer's pyre)

chariot_race.factions_note: Tertullian says the first two colours were white and red and green and blue came later; the date of the four-faction system is disputed (late Republic or early Empire). Shown as four because the brief asks; the Republic evidence is thin. Gold and purple were Domitian's (Suet. Dom. 7), not used.

laps.count_source: Imperial and later sources give seven laps (spatia); Republican figure not read
laps.counter_dolphins: seven bronze dolphins added by Agrippa in 33 BC; Dio 49.43.2
laps.counter_republic: seven eggs on a bar, one removed or turned each lap; Livy 41.27.6 (174 BC)
laps.direction: anticlockwise round the spina, turns on the left; standard modern reading of the circus layout

metae.description: three conical pillars at each end of the spina; the turn round them is the dangerous place

order: boys and youths of equestrian and citizen families, on horse and on foot, by age-class
charioteers in quadrigae and bigae and riders of single horses
athletes, naked but for a loincloth
dancers in three bands (men, youths, boys) to pipes and lyres; satyr and silenus dancers
sacred vessels of gold and silver
the images of the gods carried on shoulders (placed on the pulvinar for the games)
pompa.route: from the Capitol, through the Forum, to the Circus Maximus

pulvinar.description: the shrine-couch from which the gods' images and the presiding magistrate watched, on the Palatine side
pulvinar.source: Suet. Aug. 45 (Augustus and the pulvinar); Livy 5.13 (lectisternium, couches for the gods)

races_per_day.game_use: the animation shows one race; the programme length is the engine's choice
races_per_day.imperial: Domitian once gave 100 races in a day (Suet. Dom. 4.3, 'centum missus'); a day of 24 is the usual modern figure for the Empire

start.carceres_source: twelve is the usual modern count; Livy 41.27.6 (carceres rebuilt 174 BC) for the structure
start.signal: the presiding magistrate (editor) drops a cloth, the mappa; gates open together
start.signal_note: disputed/thin for the Republic: the mappa story is attested later (Cassiod. Var. 3.51 is the usual cite)

teams.biga: two horses; Dion. Hal. 7.72 names both

chariot_race.where: Circus Maximus (monument id circus_maximus); the Circus Flaminius also held games

ludi.founded: traditional, by Tarquinius Priscus (Livy 1.35.9; Dion. Hal. 7.71, 7.73); a regular annual feast of the republic from 366 BC (Livy 6.42.12) # date and passage unverified
ludi.note: the extension from one day to 15 over the Republic is the standard story; precise stages unverified

ludi.founded: origin uncertain; attested by Livy 23.30.17 (216 BC) # unverified
vowed 212 BC on the Marcian prophecies (Livy 25.12); made annual 208 BC (Livy 27.23.5) # unverified
ludi.note: the game year 212 BC is the vow; the first celebration is 212 BC
ludi.when: July; the date varied before fixing

ludi.founded: the stone of Cybele came to Rome in 204 BC (Livy 29.10-14); the temple was dedicated and the games set up in 191 BC (Livy 36.36.3) # unverified
ludi.note: the 204 BC date in the brief is the arrival of the goddess; the games proper begin in the 190s

ludi.founded: uncertain; plebeian aediles; Livy 30.39.8 mentions the games of 202 BC # unverified
temple of Flora vowed 241/238 BC (Pliny NH 18.286); made annual by decree of the Senate 173 BC (Ovid Fasti 5.277-330) # unverified

armatures.arms: oblong shield (scutum), visored helmet with crest, sword, greave on the left leg, short armguard on the right arm
armatures.name: samnis
armatures.source: Livy 9.40.17 (Campanians arm gladiators as Samnites, from the spoils); details of the kit from modern reconstructions

armatures.arms: large shield, helmet, sword; later called murmillo
armatures.name: gallus
armatures.source: Cicero passage not identified (unverified); the 'Gallus' name is Republican, murmillo is the Imperial name

armatures.arms: small square shield (parmula), curved sword (sica), greaves
armatures.name: thraex
armatures.source: attested late Republic (Spartacus is called a Thracian, Plut. Crassus 8); details from modern reconstructions

munus.armatures_note: retiarius, secutor and others are Imperial; not shown

bout.gesture_note: disputed: the raised finger (ad digitum) is Imperial evidence (Martial Spect. 29), and the 'thumb' signal (pollex verso, Juvenal 3.36) is ambiguous. The game shows a raised finger and a hand sign only as the engine's decision.
bout.missio_source: Cic. Tusc. 2.41; Cic. Pro Rabirio Post. 17 # both unverified
bout.sequence: pairs matched by arms; the fight until one is wounded or yields
bout.stroke: the loser was expected to take the sword without flinching; Cic. Tusc. 2.41
bout.yield: a beaten man grounded his shield and raised a finger; the editor, swayed by the crowd, gave missio (let him live) or the sign for the stroke

origin.what: first gladiators in Rome, three pairs in the Forum Boarium at the funeral of D. Junius Brutus Pera, given by his sons
60 men for P. Licinius, three days

munus.origin_nature: a funeral duty (munus) owed to the dead, given privately by the heirs until the later Republic

people.editor: the giver of the games; sits with the stands' best seats and gives the sign; Republic: a private citizen or magistrate
people.lanista: the trainer-dealer who owned and hired out the troupe; Cic. Pro Sestio 134 (gladiators and lanistae)

where.amphitheatre: first stone amphitheatre 29 BC, Statilius Taurus, Dio 51.23.1 (Campus Martius)
where.republic: in the Forum, between the temporary wooden stands (spectaculum); Vitruvius 5.1.1 on the oblong Forum made for gladiatorial shows; Plut. C. Gracchus 12 on the seats

sacrifice.favourable_signs: favourable: exta whole, liver clean; unfavourable: the head of the liver missing, or a defect
sacrifice.prayer_paraphrase: Father Mars, we pray that you keep this farm, our household and our flock safe and well, and take this offering in the proper way. If it is not right, we shall do it again.

steps.source: Plut. Quaest. Rom. 10 (veiled head, Roman rite); Dion. Hal. 7.72
steps.what: the magistrate (head veiled with the toga), attendants, the victim led to the altar before the temple, flute-player (tibicen) playing
led with a slack rope, a sign it comes willingly; white for Jupiter, with gilded horns for a great sacrifice
before the god in question was named, Janus and Vesta were invoked first; wine and incense offered

steps.source: Festus s.v. immolare, Servius on Ecl. 8.82 # unverified
steps.what: salted spelt-meal sprinkled on the victim's head, a knife drawn along the back

steps.source: Cato Agr. 132 (porca praecidanea), 134 (Janus, Jupiter, Juno), 139 (grove), 141 (Mars Pater, suovetaurilia)
steps.what: the formula spoken by the magistrate and echoed word for word; paraphrased from Cato
the popa stunned with a hammer or axe, the cultrarius cut the throat
the liver, heart, lungs and gall-bladder drawn out and read; sound organs mean the god accepts (litatio); a defect means the sacrifice is repeated
the god's portion (the exta) roasted on the altar; the rest eaten

division.formula: pedibus in sententiam ire, 'to go by foot to a proposal'
division.name: discessio, 'going apart': those for the proposal went and stood on one side, those against on the other, and were counted
division.note: voice-vote opinions came first, the division after; the game plays only the division

session.chair: the presiding magistrate on a curule chair on the tribunal at the far end; senators sit on benches along the side walls (the Curia Julia had three tiers)
session.daylight: no decree after sunset; Gellius 14.7.8 # unverified
session.order_of_speaking: by rank: the princeps senatus, then consulars, then praetorians and so on; in the late Republic the consuls-designate were asked first (Gellius 4.10.1)
session.relatio: the presiding magistrate lays the matter before the house (referre ad senatum)
session.seats_note: the 'three broad steps each side' is the Curia Julia as excavated; the Republican Curia Hostilia is not known in detail
session.size: about 300 senators in the middle Republic; 600 under Sulla; 900 under Caesar
session.veto: a tribune could stop the matter by intercessio

summons.auspices: the magistrate took the auspices the same morning, before the meeting
summons.place: only in a templum, a place inaugurated: the Curia (Hostilia, later Julia), temples such as Jupiter Stator, Concordia, Bellona
summons.who: a consul, a praetor or a tribune of the plebs (an interrex too)

triumph.conditions: decree of the Senate; a general with imperium; a conventional minimum of 5,000 enemy dead (Val. Max. 2.8.1 # unverified)

end.sacrifice: at the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus the general lays his laurel on Jupiter's lap and sacrifices oxen; the captive leaders, if condemned, were killed at the foot of the Capitol

order.what: the Senate and magistrates lead the way
wagons of captured arms, statues and pictures, gold and silver, carried in carts and on poles; labelled with the names of cities taken
white oxen with gilded horns and garlands, for the sacrifice, with attendants

order.source: Plut. Aem. 33 (Perseus and his children); Josephus BJ 7.153-155
order.what: captive chiefs and kings in chains with their families
lictors with laurel-wreathed fasces, in red tunics

order.source: Plut. Aem. 34; Livy 10.7.9; Pliny NH 33.111 (red paint); Pliny NH 28.39 (slave, fascinum); Tertullian Apol. 33
order.what: the general in the quadriga with four horses, laurel crown, face painted red, embroidered purple toga (toga picta) and palm-embroidered tunic, holding laurel and a sceptre; a public slave behind holds the crown and whispers that he is a man
white horses; Camillus (396 BC) was criticised for using them
soldiers in order by unit, wreathed with laurel, singing and shouting 'Io triumphe', and singing rude songs at the general

triumph.order_note: Plut. Aem. 32-34 describes the triumph of L. Aemilius Paullus (167 BC) over three days; Josephus BJ 7.123-157 is Vespasian and Titus in AD 71 (a parallel, Imperial); Appian Pun. 66 is Scipio's triumph (201 BC).

route.disputed: the exact route is disputed (the Velabrum and Circus Maximus before the Via Sacra is the usual reconstruction; Coarelli, Östenberg); the Porta Triumphalis's location is uncertain
route.source: Josephus BJ 7.130-131 (Vespasian); Plut. Aem. 32; Cic. Pis. 55 # all unverified
stages: assembly on the Campus Martius (the general cannot enter the pomerium before)
the Circus Flaminius and the theatres where the crowd stood
the Clivus Capitolinus to the Capitol and the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
